body.text: Cuba After Castro, a documentary produced by BreakThrough News, a US-based news outlet, arrives in Fidel Castro’s birth centenary year. Directed by Matthew Belen and Abby Martin, it takes on the task of profiling Miguel Díaz-Canel, Cuba’s first leader born after the Revolution, while capturing how his leadership has prepared the country for the US’ mounting hostility. The film also trains its lens on the present: how Cuba’s current generations relate to the Revolution they inherited. For all its focus on the present, Fidel’s shadow stretches across the film.

In its portrayal of Díaz-Canel, Cuba After Castro does not attempt a charismatic makeover; instead, it paints a very human picture of the President, shaped by his quiet temperament and political vision. The documentary is candid about this trait: that he keeps a low profile and is relatively less visible than Fidel Castro.

Fidel set the bar impossibly high, not just for his successor but also for any leader across the world. The voluble revolutionary leader holds the record for the longest speech ever made at the United Nations—4 hours and 29 minutes. After the National Assembly re-elected him to a five-year term as President in February 1998, Fidel delivered one of his longest speeches—7 hours and 30 minutes. Gabriel García Márquez, in “A Personal Portrait of Fidel”, captured this quality perfectly: “weary of talking, he rests by talking.”

When the camera moves back to Díaz-Canel, he stays true to his personality and wastes no time in drawing out his understanding of the Cuban Revolution. As someone who grew up watching the Revolution, Díaz-Canel had his first brush with the revolutionary leader in eighth grade. There is bonus footage in the film of Díaz-Canel operating a lathe machine as a 13-year-old. A graduate in electrical engineering, he began his political career as a member of the Young Communist League. He slowly rose through the ranks over the years: from becoming a member of the Central Committee to the Politburo, to holding the Higher Education Ministry, to Vice President, to now. Díaz-Canel’s current and final tenure comes to an end in 2028. He speaks in a self-aware manner about the duties expected of him.

As Díaz-Canel explains how all essential economic activities were under the control of US conglomerates, archival footage of Fulgencio Batista, the cruelties of his regime, and newspaper cuttings help visualise and situate his descriptions.

The documentary’s lens zooms out to frame the broader image of Latin American history. Díaz-Canel recalls his time in Nicaragua as an international collaborator during the Sandinista revolution, and the film traces a pattern that extends far beyond Cuba: the Dominican Republic, where the US intervened in 1965 to prevent the formation of a communist government; Chile in 1973; El Salvador in 1979; Grenada in 1983; Panama in 1989; among others. From the record, Díaz-Canel draws the conclusion: “Cuba has every reason to denounce US foreign policy.”

US attention and aggression towards Cuba did not start with Fidel. The third US President, Thomas Jefferson, called the island “the most interesting addition which could ever be made to our system of States”. He tried buying Cuba from Spain in 1808 but failed. The US tried again in 1848 and 1854. In 1898, when the island nation, after years of struggle, tried to liberate itself from the Spanish empire, the US intervened, again. After the signing of the Treaty of Paris, the US, through the 1901 Platt Amendment, ensured control over the island.

Alongside the decades-old Torricelli Act and Helms-Burton Act, brought in to cripple Cuba, Donald Trump, the film notes, introduced 243 new restrictions on Cuba during his first term, including returning the country to the list of state sponsors of terrorism.
Parallel documentaries and Cuba After Castro

Many documentaries on Cuba dwell on the hardships endured by its people, yet a few identify their root cause so directly: US imperialism, decades of economic sanctions, and an interventionist doctrine that sought to strangle the island. Fewer still ask how, against such crippling odds, Cuba managed to forge a distinct identity in healthcare.

Take, for instance, the US filmmaker Michael Moore’s 2007 documentary Sicko, which drew a contrast between American and Cuban healthcare. The film’s portrayal of Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital providing accessible medical treatment to everyone was more than what the US Interests Section in Havana could bear. It sent a cable to the US State Department saying the Cuban government had suppressed Sicko. Moore countered it through a blog article, noting that the entire nation of Cuba had been shown the film on national television on April 28, 2008, a most fitting rebuttal.

The humanitarian cost of US hostility came to the surface at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when the island appealed to the US government to authorise the sale of oxygen to Cuba. Díaz-Canel pauses and says, “The US never responded.” Worse, he says his government holds evidence that the US pressured Latin American companies and Caribbean countries not to sell oxygen to Cuba. Díaz-Canel sharply calls out the dehumanising act.

Cuba did not wait for the vaccine donations to save its people; it developed its own vaccines. Díaz-Canel fills with pride when he says Cuba is the smallest country in the world to develop its own vaccine.

The magnitude of the US’ apathy is reflected in the 2025 study in The Lancet Global Health, which said unilateral sanctions imposed by the US and EU from 1970 to 2021 are associated with 38 million deaths worldwide. In 2021 alone, they were associated with more than 8,00,000 deaths.

Documentaries like the BBC’s Fidel Castro: America’s Nemesis (2016) bluntly open with a verdict: “His was a dictatorship that lasted more than 50 years.” Cuba After Castro answers differently without any defensiveness. Fidel’s wish, Díaz-Canel recalls, was that even his grave carry no commemorative inscription. In December 2016, Raúl Castro announced that no street or public monument in Cuba would bear his brother’s name. A dictator, the film implies, does not resist the cult himself.

In his elaborate breakdown of Cuba’s electoral processes in Cuba After Castro, Díaz-Canel summarises, “A political system chosen by a country, supported by the people, must start from a historical vision, from the roots and culture of that country. It has to do with the way in which [José] Martí saw the need for the Cuban Revolutionary Party to win the war against the Spanish.”

Yet Cuba After Castro does not dwell on the glory of the Revolution and the country’s resilience alone. It also registers the expectations of those who see no end to the ongoing struggle. It captures a public meeting in the municipality of Santa Clara, where voters meet their candidates before the election and raise their concerns in the President’s physical presence. As many pledge to defend and uphold the Revolution, one man speaks of fuel shortages and crumbling infrastructure. Visibly emotional, he asks: “What good are our contributions if the most any of us can do is beg?” Díaz-Canel’s eyes well up.

Al Jazeera’s Invent and Resolve documentary meticulously talks about how Cubans recycle, reuse, and repurpose their household appliances for their evolving needs. It features historians and experts who explain the harshness of the embargo. It also packs Fidel’s anti-imperialist speeches to strengthen its narrative.

There are also documentaries like ARTE.tv’s Cuba: An Island in Turmoil. It tracks the rise of MIPYMES (micro, small, and medium enterprises) in the island nation after 2021 to help revive the economy devastated by the pandemic, hyperinflation, and a collapse in tourism. However, except for a fleeting reference to the US embargo, it largely portrays Cuba’s crisis as an inevitable result of its planned economy. It presents the issues of crumbling infrastructure, power cuts, and empty medical shops as abstract manifestations, delinking them from the political and moral accountability of the US.
The press and the protests

When asked why Cuba prohibits private media ownership while it allows other private businesses, Díaz-Canel responds: “Private media outlets respond to a very class-based and very specific interest of those who fund those outlets.”

When Martin poses a question about the July 11, 2021, protests across Cuba, Díaz-Canel points to the intense campaigns organised by the US in the run-up to the 2021 protests. “In the same year, several countries like Colombia, Thailand, and Palestine also faced protests, but somehow protests in Cuba alone are propagated majorly by media.”

The journalist N.P. Ullekh’s book Mad About Cuba lends weight to the claim, citing the former Central Intelligence Agency analyst Fulton Armstrong: the protests, “while rooted in authentic demands”, were “well-planned” with US support.

In 2025, for the 33rd consecutive year, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution calling for an end to the decades-long United States embargo against Cuba. An overwhelming majority of countries voted in favour, as always. Speaking of the “Special Period”, after the disintegration of the USSR, Díaz-Canel says those years left the country “with many wounds that have not yet healed, and they are now appearing as consequences of the era in which we live”. His words carry the emotional weight of Cuba bearing the longest-running economic embargo in the world.

"Fifty-plus years of animosity, embargo, rationing. And Fidel Castro is still hanging on. But recently there are powerful indications that everything is about to change.” So ends the travel documentarian Anthony Bourdain’s Parts Unknown episode on Cuba, which aired in 2015. Eleven years on, the change he sensed has not come, and the threat to Cuba looms larger than ever. In the tenth year since Fidel’s death, Cuba After Castro shows the spirit of Fidel Castro and the Cuban Revolution still standing watch over its people.
